author: The Best Advisory
text:
A hard week for a lot of people in legal.

Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP plans to wind down after 95 years, and around 2,000 people are now facing news most of them never saw coming. 

First years who had only just started, the teams who keep a firm running day to day, people who built whole careers there. Whatever the headlines say about partners & strategy, this is a really tough week for a lot of good people, and our thoughts are with every one of them. If you're hiring, now is a good time to say so.

And legal tech didn't stand still. Clio gave practice management an AI makeover in Boston,

Claude has ready-made tools built for lawyers, and Anthropic has filed to go public. Not content with that, it's also reportedly backing its own AI consultancy, so the AI lab now wants to do the advising too. As an advisory ourselves, we'll be watching that one closely 👀

Big week, lots to be excited about, as long as we 
remember it's people who make any of it work.

Happy Friday  ✨

pageImages.alt: Behind every headline are people. The biggest legal story this week wasn’t about AI. It was about who stays, who goes and who saw it coming. Source: Above the Law, 28 October; Artificial Lawyer, 29 October 2026

Most of them didn’t see it coming. Around 2,000 people at Weil Gotshal. Associates, first years who had only just joined, secretaries, paralegals, BD, IT and innovation teams. Most won’t be in the headlines. If you’re hiring, this is a good week to say so. Source: Above the Law, 28 October; Axios, 29 October 2026

It wasn’t AI. It was people. Artificial Lawyer is clear AI played no part. Top partners left for more profitable firms, merger talks fell through and others followed. A firm is only as strong as the people who choose to stay. Source: Artificial Lawyer, 29 October 2026

Practice management, meet AI. At ClioCon in Boston, Clio showed one platform with AI throughout, agentic workflows and its own AI phone system. The tool you already use is becoming your AI tool. Source: Legal IT Insider, 26 October; LawSites, 29 October 2026

Less prompting, more doing. Anthropic launched ready‑made legal tools in Claude, from cite checks to matter boards, plus 60+ legal connectors. Claude does the first pass. Your lawyers still sign. Source: Anthropic, 28 October 2026

author: Sophie Best
text:
The more I speak to GCs the more this question comes up.

I actually think there is an argument for both sides it’s not as easy as AI means costs are cut.

Take law firms, tech is expensive. Then training and checking.

But it is clear legal teams want transparency on what tech does mean for workflows and time billed.

The one way to make this a less difficult conversation? Find ways to add more value with the AI you use.

This way the cost comes less into question or changes the way it’s discussed.

quotedPost.text:
60% of in-house teams now expect lower fees when their firms use AI
54% say AI has already cut the work they send out.

That conversation is coming to every partner sooner or later. Discounting the hours AI removed is the easy answer & the weakest one, because it only ever goes one way. 

The firms that come out of this well will know exactly which steps of a matter AI changed, & will have something better to offer than a smaller bill.

When a client asks what AI saved them, what’s your answer?

pageImages.alt: 60% of in‑house teams expect lower fees when firms use AI. 54% say AI has already cut the work they send out. Source: Everlaw & Wakefield Research, 300 US in‑house professionals, Oct 2026
Your client thinks AI cut your hours. So when the invoice looks the same as last year, what’s the answer?

72% → 44% of legal work billed by the hour, today vs in two to three years. That’s legal leaders’ own forecast. 78% say cost reduction is what they want from their firms’ use of AI. Source: Deloitte, The AI Imperative, 121 senior legal leaders, Jul 2026

Start with what AI actually changed. When we run workflow sessions in firms as part of our academy, we start with one question: which steps of the matter did AI change? Most teams can’t answer it yet. You can’t offer clients more until you can.
One question for law firm partners When a client asks what AI saved them, what’s your answer? A discount, or a better service they couldn’t buy before?

author: Sophie Best
text:
I get asked which tool to buy all the time. Almost nobody asks who they’re buying it from. 
  
I talk a lot about shiny tools & sorting your data out first, because bad in, bad out. Both still stand, but who you're actually buying from gets far less airtime. Every provider will tell you they're a partner & most of them mean it. 
  
An F1 car is extraordinary engineering right up until you get in and realise you don't know how to drive it. Legal tech is pretty much the same. The technology matters but it rarely decides whether it works. 
  
The questions I'd ask anyone before signing: 

Who will you actually be dealing with in month three, not the sales team? 
Is there someone to call who understands legal workflows, not just password resets? 
Will they help you build a playbook? AI in contracting is only as good as your clause library. 
What's the plan for the first ninety days? A vendor will describe implementation, a partner will describe what happens after it. 
  
Chatting to Alexandria (Lexi) Lutz, GC at contract intelligence system Summize, about exactly this at London’s LegalTechTalk!

As a GC she's been on the buying side too. "No in-house team I know started with a playbook. The partner helped us build ours, the vendor sent a template. And after go-live I needed numbers for the board, not anecdotes." Their clients say the same. One team of two said "We're just two people and we need a super strong support partnership", that's the reality for so many in-house teams. It's why who you can call matters more than the demo. 
  
The other one is whether it properly sits inside the everyday tools your team already lives in, not 3 million buttons to get there... 
  
Another GC, another legal team. They'd bought a contract and matter management tool for efficiency, oversight and, above all, reporting, so they could finally show the business what legal was doing. On paper it was fine. Yet hardly anyone used it, and they couldn't work out why. 
  
I asked them to show me their day to day, and it clicked. It didn't connect to anything they worked in, so every email, matter and contract had to be entered by hand. A tool bought to save lawyers time was asking them for data entry. That isn't a training problem. It's a blocker, and no amount of encouragement fixes it. 
  
The lesson for anyone buying, ask how it fits the way your team already works before you ask what it can do!

author: The Best Advisory
text:
A demo shows you the product. A trial shows you the fit 👀

Sophie Best has seen similar patterns with clients again and again. A shiny tool looks perfect in the demo, then can struggle once it meets the team’s real work

The complex contracts, the existing systems, the way people actually draft, review and sign off. 

Nobody tested that properly, because the evaluation stopped at the demo.

A proper trial is a simulation of how your team really works, run on your hardest tasks by the lawyers who will use the tool every day. Map five use cases as they work today and ask the vendor to set each one up. Check it works inside the systems you already use. Then ask the governance questions before you sign, not after.

Go live is the start, not the finish.

Who will own it after launch? Who will run training and change management?

Want help or advise with the process? Drop us a message 👇

pageImages.alt: Legal Technology Evaluation Checklist W H A T T O A S K B E F O R E , D U R I N G A N D A F T E R A D E M O

A trial is not a quick test. It’s a real simulation of how your team works, on your most complex contracts and tasks, under an NDA and data agreement, run by the lawyers who will use it every day. How it handles your hardest work tells you more than any demo can.

Does it fit how you work? 0 1 Have you mapped five use cases as they work today, and asked them to set each up? 0 2 Does it work inside Word, Outlook and your DMS, with your permissions? 0 3 Does it handle your jurisdictions, laws and languages? 0 4 Will a real team build your playbook from your positions?

Then ask the governance questions. 0 1 Where will your data be stored, and is that allowed for your clients and regulators? 0 2 Are prompts and outputs kept, and is any of it used for training? 0 3 Which AI model sits underneath, and can that change? 0 4 Can you take your data and playbooks with you if you leave?
One question for in‑house teams Who will own it after launch? Go live is the start, not the finish. Someone has to own the training, the feedback and the playbook as your work changes.

You pretty much are switched on constantly. The smile doesn’t leave.

Rushing to the bathroom, stopped on the way but too polite so you stop and have the conversation. After all I have immense appreciation for people who step out their comfort zone here and actually try to interact.

I know some of you hover at the back but that gets zero connection 😉

I’ll forever be grateful for firms granting me the space to talk at these. Especially when it’s things I’m so passionate about. The future of legal. How we can responsibly roll out tech & AI. No doom & gloom just how to approach it and move forward.

But these days I also 💯look after my mental health. Something I never would have done whilst in corporate or junior.

So yesterday after a fantastic two days and 30 minutes before the airport pick up I shut the laptop and headed to the spa. Anyone who knows Jumeirah hotels will know Talise is the creme de la creme!

quotedPost.text:
Copilot checked it 👀

That could soon be why a supplier agreement never reaches legal.

Microsoft has launched Copilot for legal, with more than 20 legal skills built into Word, and they are on by default for every Microsoft 365 Copilot commercial licence holder, not just the legal team.

That’s also what makes it so useful. 
There’s no new platform to learn, no new login. 

The legal skills sit inside Word, the tool lawyers already work in all day, and Cowork carries them across the emails, meetings and files they already have in Microsoft 365. 

As Microsoft's own counsel put it, the real benefit is not having to change how you work.

But Microsoft's own documentation also says no output should be relied on without review by a qualified legal professional. The question is whether the rest of the business knows that, and whether there is a clear route back to legal when it matters.

This is not a reason to switch it off. It is a reason for legal to set the rules before the business sets its own.

Who outside legal will use this first?

author: Sophie Best
text:
Everyone thinks they need AI. Most teams I meet need structure 

Ask an in-house team which AI tool they're looking at and they'll tell you. Ask which problem costs the business most and it goes quiet.

It goes quiet because teams get marketed features, rarely their own challenges or what solving them would open up.

Was talking to Alexandria (Lexi) Lutz GC at Summize at LegalTechTalk. She was also saying how overwhelmed in-house teams are feeling. The market's flooded with AI, the demos all look similar, and teams have almost forgotten why they were looking for tech in the first place, because they had a problem to solve.

She's right, and nobody says it out loud. 
Even working out who to talk to is a job in itself.

Then the myths. That AI will fix a process nobody has defined. That the tool with the best demo is the best tool. That buying is the hard part. None of them survive contact with a real legal team.

Then the confusion underneath, which is worse. CLM? Contract AI? Drafting? Review? A repository? The categories overlap and nobody explains them.

So decisions get made off the demo not a mapped-out assessment. Not because GCs are careless, because the market gives them no neutral way to compare and the demo is all that feels concrete. I've watched capable teams do it.
In my experience what most in-house teams are missing is not intelligence. It is structure. 

Knowing what you have, where it lives, what it commits you to, and being able to answer a question about it without three days of searching.

It looks different for every team, which is the point. 

For some it’s renewals and expiries, the agreement that quietly lapsed. For others its obligations, notice periods, volume commitments, price reviews and auto renewals unopened since signature. 

For some it's governance, evidencing what was agreed, by whom, under what authority, when someone finally asks.

For some it's speed under pressure. A conflict, sanctions, a supply chain failure, and the first question is which contracts are affected. Most can't answer quickly, and slowly is much the same as not at all. 

For many, it's simply visibility. 
Sales has a pipeline the CFO can see. 
What does legal have? 

If you can't extract it as data, you can't put a graph in a board pack, and legal stays invisible where budget gets decided.

Was chatting to a GC who was being pitched contract AI, but the real headache was their main supply agreement. It had expired and nobody noticed until a shipment didn't turn up. No model was fixing that. Knowing what they had and when it ran out would have. And what were they being pitched? A drafting tool, for a team that mostly reviews other people's paper.

Sometimes the shiny tool is genuinely the right one. The problem is not the demo, it is not knowing why it is right for you before you sign.

Know your problem first and every demo becomes a test, not a pitch.

If you're in-house, which of these is costing you most right now?

author: Sophie Best
text:
The problem with comparing legal work today with legal work a year ago? 

It’s no longer a like for like comparison.

I think this is one of the things we’re still getting wrong when we talk about AI and the legal profession.

Falcon is a good example. The newly launched AI-native law firm is offering up to six commercial contract reviews a month for €1,000, with same-day turnaround and each review signed off by a qualified lawyer. 

That works out at around €170 per review. Falcon compares that with €3–4k at a traditional firm.

You can debate that comparison, and I’m sure people will 👀

But I think we’re missing the point underneath it.

The economics of producing legal work are changing.

A contract review supported by AI isn’t simply the same piece of work done a little faster. 

Different process. Different amount of human time required. Different cost of producing it. 

And, increasingly, the client’s expectation of what that work should cost will be different too.

Yet we’re still trying to measure that against how legal work has traditionally been delivered.

Often where some of the pessimism around AI and the legal profession comes from. We take today’s capabilities, apply them to yesterday’s operating model, and ask what gets displaced.

What happens to the lawyer who used to spend five hours doing this?

But perhaps the better question is: if we were designing that service from scratch today, would we ever design it around five hours of lawyer time in the first place?

That doesn’t mean lawyers disappear. It means we become much more deliberate about where lawyers actually add value, judgement, strategy, complexity, relationships. And where technology can change the way the underlying work is delivered.

And this isn’t really about whether Falcon’s €170 comparison is right or wrong.

It’s about what happens when new models start giving clients a completely different benchmark for what routine legal work can cost. Their pricing may be aimed at startups and SMEs today, but published prices don’t stay neatly within one part of the market. They become reference points.

And that’s why I don’t think we can keep benchmarking what comes next against what came before.

It’s not like for like anymore.

Excited to be back up on stage this week supporting Morae on a UAE roadshow. Are you joining us? Dima Godfrey

author: Sophie Best
text:
18 working days to two hours 👀

That's what the UAE Ministry of Justice says its new AI does to pre-trial case analysis.

It uses six autonomous agents that read the docket, cross-reference the submissions & hand the judge a structured brief and was unveiled at the UN Crime Congress in Abu Dhabi.

The day before, in the same building, 119 countries had adopted a declaration promising four things about AI in criminal justice: human oversight, transparency, traceability & personal data protection.

I'm not going to pretend that's a contradiction, because it isn't. The commitment arrives first, the measurement catches up later, which is the normal order of things. It’s the same order I watch play out inside companies most weeks.

But those four words are far more useful than they look 👀

Three of them are things a buyer can ask for evidence of today, from any vendor, without waiting for anyone to write a rule. 

Traceable means a retained record of which sources an output drew on & which version of the model produced it. 

Human oversight means a named person, a defined decision they own & a log showing they actually exercised it, rather than a tick box at the bottom of a policy nobody has opened since it was signed off.

AI Governance & what keeps the GC up at night is what we’re working through at the roundtable in Abu Dhabi next week.

The GCs I speak to aren't behind on any of this. They're being asked to prove something nobody designed the system to record, & that's a very different problem from the one most people think they have.

119 countries have just handed you the vocabulary. The rest is procurement ✨

author: Sophie Best
text:
OpenAI released Astra for Law this week my feed is full of it. 

Spoiler: every legal AI launch gets the same reaction 👀

Most don’t ask the question that matters.

What clients tend to ask me isn't whether it's fit for purpose. It's whether it's fit for OUR purpose.

Different question entirely. It means knowing what you actually need before you go looking. Most teams skip straight past it.

The numbers are also worth knowing. OpenAI reported 54.0% overall correctness on 200 US legal research questions from Vals AI's benchmark, against 38.7% for the same model using web search alone. Their own test, highest reasoning effort.

Let’s remember this is a race. One to more capability & faster. But a launch is their milestone, not yours. It lands on their timeline & their commercial pressures, & neither of those knows anything about your work.

Two of my clients this month explain what I mean.

One is deep in compliance & sanctions. Vessels coming into port, what they can actually know about them, which regulation bites & when. The other is transaction heavy & corporate, wanting red flag due diligence across a due diligence pack without three associates losing a weekend to it.

Which is where it gets specific to you. Whether it does know your use cases. Whether it knows your jurisdictions or you can feed them in. Whether you buy it or build around your own precedent, because Sullivan & Cromwell, Ropes & Gray & Cooley each built their own tools on top of it with OpenAI engineers in the room, most firms don't have that option.

My phone helpfully reminded me of the Asian Legal Business Middle East In-House Legal Summit with Thomson Reuters MENA last year. I sat on a panel with some other brilliant legal minds for “Beyond Automation, on building a future-ready legal tech strategy for in-house teams in the MENA region”. The title did most of the work. Nobody on that stage wanted to talk about which product was best. The conversation was about how you understand your own organisation, how you map the problem before you go shopping, who actually gets trained, & what the workflow looks like on a Tuesday afternoon when someone is under deadline.

None of that changed this week. It won't change with the next launch either.

The teams who get this right aren't just the ones watching the launches. They're the ones who already know what they're looking for when one lands.

author: Sophie Best
text:
Four steps forward. Five steps back.

1921 - Women banned from playing on FA-affiliated grounds in England. The ban held for fifty years.

1984 - The first women's Olympic marathon. Before that, the official line was that our bodies would break.

2026 - Novig, a sports betting app, puts Sydney Sweeney on screen naked, has her repeat the word "sports", & that’s representation.

Before anyone starts: this isn't about policing what a woman does with her body. She can do what she likes.

It's about what the ad is doing.

I know what comes next. It's not that deep. It is that deep.

43% of teenage girls who once thought of themselves as sporty drop out of sport after primary school. For boys it's 24%. 68% say a fear of being judged is what stops them.

I'm not an athlete by any means. But I am massively into sport. I don't do it for aesthetics, I do it because it makes me feel good, sharper even.

I can lift 70+ kilos over my head. I can back squat 100. I've run a marathon & a half. I've done Hyrox races. What women’s body can do is impressive and it’s more than just looks. Which is the whole point.

We have always had to fight for our space. Professionally & personally. Women athletes have been doing this for years.

Think about the young girls deciding right now whether sport is for them, what this tells them: unless you look like a model, it isn't.

And she isn't the face they hired. She has equity in this business. She knew exactly what she was signing.

Really, really sad. And utter ********, with a capital B.

Women in sports deserve more

author: Sophie Best
text:
Sam Altman says he sees a future where intelligence is a utility. Like water or electricity. Bought from them on a meter. Read that again 👀

Meanwhile people are walking out of the companies building this stuff & telling everyone the odds aren't good.

So is the world actually going to end 👀

I don't think it's over. But I've been having this conversation on panels for years & what people keep missing is everything that goes wrong long before we get anywhere near an ending.

Just because you can doesn't mean you should.

Meanwhile we're all still arguing about whether it got the clause right or is taking all jobs…

Yes. We know that. It makes things up. That's the low hanging stuff.

What I'm talking about is what happens when it has an actual social impact. If a judge & a representation team are working from information that's been fed with biased data, then AI has the ability to make that worse.

So back to the people walking away.

Geoffrey Irving was chief scientist at the UK's AI Security Institute & worked at DeepMind & OpenAI before that. He's just put the chance of all of us dying as a result of superintelligence at around 50%.

I don't think they're trying to scare us in the sense of the film where it's over in a day. I think they're trying to tell us there's a problem.

Suzanne Natalie Jeffers & I put the world to right on a late night chat on this & someone made a point nobody has answered. Food gets tested before it's released. So do drugs. There's a whole process before any of it hits the market.

Why is AI not like that?

We do regulate AI. But nearly all of it applies after release & nothing stops a new model shipping first & being looked at later. Strange gap when we're this careful about a new painkiller.

And it isn't hypothetical. In July an OpenAI model being tested on a hacking benchmark got itself out of the sandbox it was meant to be sealed inside & broke into Hugging Face's live systems to get the answers to the test it was sitting. The safety filters had been switched off on purpose for that evaluation. But nobody told it to break into anyone's servers. It worked out that was the quickest way to win.

And we're still arguing about whether it takes our jobs.

These things are already in hiring & hospitals & courts & travel. So what happens when one goes off course somewhere like air traffic control? I'm not scaremongering. I just think people need to think about what the impact of this actually is.

I'll be honest. I don't think these companies give a flying crap. They're in a race & only one of them gets to be first.

And businesses exist to make money. I'm not naive about that.

You can't supply water or electricity to a single household without licensing & safety standards & a regulator checking before it reaches anyone. That's what being a utility means.

He wants the meter. Just not the rest of it.

We get regulated for everything else. So why not this?

Just because you can doesn't mean you should ✨

author: Sophie Best
text:
What a week ✨

2 hours of training for DIFC Academy on their laws course upskilling on AI & legaltech

HP Nova training to teachers on how AI is impacting the workforce in real time 

A panel discussion on velocity for LexTalk World. This time not just about AI but how a GC navigates the enterprise trust and risk in a disrupted world.

Some of the talk tracks 👇

Horizon scanning is only useful if you can turn intelligence into action. With sanctions, trade controls, regulatory changes privacy anyone… constant changes mean legal teams need to connect these to their own data, jurisdictions, counterparties & contracts. And then into workflows that answer:

What changed?
Does it affect us?
Who owns it? Who should own it? 
What happens next?

On shortening deal cycles. Because hello AI use 👀

Don’t start with the AI. Start with where the deal is actually getting stuck. Intake? Drafting? Redlines? Approvals? 

On AI governance and more:

Not every AI use case carries the same risk. Improving a generic presentation with publicly available info is very different to uploading sensitive M&A docs, source code, personal data etc.

Legal teams need more practical advice for the business vs hefty AI policies no one understands….

Governance has to be useable. If the approved route is impossibly cumbersome people will try to go around it.

And another day of DIFC meetings 🙏

Is it Friday yet 👀

author: Sophie Best
text:
Today was a slightly different educating one.

Thanks to Tannya Jajal & AIDEN I did a guest cameo to provide some education to teachers via the HP Nova programme.

Few things we covered:

AI doesn’t replace learning, louder for the back please 👀

AI makes anyone knowledgable, it doesn’t make everyone understand.

Using AI isn’t the issue. Using it blindly is.

Retrieving information is easy. Verifying it is key. They are two completely different skills.

The people who thrive will be those who adapt and use AI not only to retrieve but to ask why it’s telling them something and to use judgement on this.

Teachers actually have this instinct already. These skills just have to be taught even more deliberately now and we have to teach how to use AI in a responsible way.

Giving up my time is always made worthwhile when you recieve screenshots of the comments I didn’t actually see properly during my talk 🙏

On a mission to demystify AI always ✨

author: Sophie Best
text:
This one’s a favour for any Dubai lawyers out there with kids interested in football.

Or maybe ones who aren’t interested but would like to be 👀

Anyone remember being “un-sporty” as a kid not because you didn’t want to but because you weren’t in the top 10%? The ones who got left on the line as everyone else got chosen for teams.

I’ve seen in it in gyms here even. Everyone focuses on the best, the fastest. The ones who will make it. The “athletes”

But let’s face it 80 plus percent are just the normal kids who want to enjoy themselves. 

Then look at real education, not just the how to kick a call but the strength training to not get injured. Teen girls on how their menstrual cycle affects everything, fuelling for performance not for aesthetics. 

That’s why I know Provn Academy will thrive as it’s been built by the best I know. Doctor Shefali Verma. She’s got two football mad girls and yet sees the issues in the sport for all kids. I’ve lost count of the times she’s told me they aren’t just small boys. 

I had a chance to play a tiny part in the summer camp they ran helping out in a few ways. Saw first hand the kids who were shy and almost maybe even didn’t want to be there change by the end of the week as they had a safe space.

Take a look at what they’re building as I don’t think you’d regret having your child try it out. 

This is something I have no affiliation or benefit from fyi just something I’ve believed in for the longest time.

Although may be found at the side lines occasionally as a back up support now I’ve done my child safety courses and. Don’t worry though I’ll be no where near the footballs. The girls have told me a few times “auntie soph you weren’t lying when you said you weren’t great at kicking the ball” 🤣” They can also run way faster than me….

Link in the comments to find out more or DM Shefali…

Doctor Shefali Verma I’m so so proud of you 🫶
